RagShortTexts: Linked metal rings need repairs at breaks and seams; padding affects wear and protection.
Mail takes skilled labor and upkeep beyond the means of many ordinary fighters.

Variants.Content: Mail could protect Rus retainers, wealthy knights and steppe elites, with ownership shaped by wealth and supply. Small linked rings place strain on rivets and seams, and a break burdens neighboring links. Flexible armor still weighs on its wearer and needs fitted clothing and padding; a protected fighter can still suffer injury from a blow.

A wearer checks armpits, shoulders and openings, where broken links can snag cloth and enlarge a tear. Sweat and rain leave mail damp, requiring care and repairs at rest; wet padding chafes. After fighting, bruising and restricted movement matter alongside penetration when deciding whether a man can ride on.

Equipping retainers means paying for ring making, riveting, fitting and repair as well as iron. Reused armor may fit poorly, hindering riding or shield use; craftsmen and spare links burden transport. A lord must maintain those regularly exposed to close combat before extending armor provision beyond available pay and food.

Repairers replace damaged links one by one, and haste misses weakened edges. Families selling grain for armor also need padding and repair money; inherited mail can become disputed property. Military repair demands compete with farm tools, cart fittings and harness for a smith's fuel and working time.
